title: Why Every Diabetic Needs Annual Eye Screening — and How AI Is Scaling It in India
excerpt: Diabetic retinopathy blinds millions who never see it coming. India's AI-powered MadhuNetrAI app and diaspora specialists are racing to change that.
body:
• Diabetic retinopathy affects up to 35% of the world's 589 million diabetics and is a leading cause of preventable blindness in working-age adults, with the global burden rising steadily.
  • India's AIIMS and the Armed Forces Medical Services launched MadhuNetrAI, an AI-powered screening app with over 95% detection accuracy, now being piloted at seven locations across India.
  • South Asians face elevated diabetes risk — experts urge annual dilated eye exams starting from diagnosis, as early-stage retinopathy often has no symptoms.
  • Indian-origin retinal specialists like Virginia-based Dr. Rohit Adyanthaya are leading advances in treatment and debunking dangerous myths about laser therapy and diabetic eye disease.

Diabetic retinopathy is quietly stealing the sight of millions worldwide, and the Indian diaspora faces outsized risk. With South Asians genetically predisposed to higher rates of Type 2 diabetes, ophthalmologists and public health experts are sounding the alarm: regular retinal screening is the single most effective defense against irreversible blindness, yet too few patients are getting it.

A Growing Global Crisis

An estimated 589 million adults worldwide live with diabetes, a number projected to reach 853 million by 2050, according to global health data. Diabetic retinopathy — damage to the retina's blood vessels caused by chronic high blood sugar — affects roughly 35% of this population. Sub-Saharan Africa reports the highest regional prevalence at nearly 36%, but South and Southeast Asia are not far behind at 28.4%.

The disease progresses silently. In its early stages, patients experience no symptoms. By the time vision blurs or dark spots appear, irreversible damage may have already occurred. In its most advanced form, proliferative diabetic retinopathy triggers the growth of abnormal blood vessels that can hemorrhage, scar the retina, and cause permanent blindness.

Where systematic screening programs exist — as in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and Nordic countries — diabetic retinopathy has been displaced as the leading cause of blindness in working-age adults. Where they don't, the damage accumulates unchecked.

India Bets on AI to Close the Gap

India is attempting to bridge its screening deficit with artificial intelligence. In December 2025, the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) launched MadhuNetrAI, described as India's first fully validated AI application for detecting diabetic retinopathy. The tool, developed by AIIMS's Dr. Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences in collaboration with the Ministry of Health's eHealth division and Wadhwani AI, analyzes retinal images captured by handheld fundus cameras and delivers results within seconds.

"While many AI systems for diabetic retinopathy are being built, the key issue is validation. Our model was tested on over 3,000-4,000 retinal images, screened from nearly 13,000 in total. We now have over 95% detection accuracy."

— Dr. Rohan Chawla, Retina Specialist, AIIMS RP Centre

The Armed Forces Medical Services is piloting MadhuNetrAI at seven locations — Pune, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Dharamshala, Gaya, Jorhat, and Kochi — covering metropolitan, rural, hilly, coastal, and remote regions. The system enables trained nurses and healthcare assistants to conduct community-level screening without an ophthalmologist present, while simultaneously generating real-time data on disease prevalence.

Patients identified with retinopathy are referred for diabetic management, while vision-threatening cases go directly to vitreo-retina specialists at designated district hospitals.

Debunking Dangerous Myths

Misconceptions about diabetic eye disease continue to delay treatment. Indian-origin retinal specialist Dr. Rohit Adyanthaya, a Virginia Eye Consultants ophthalmologist who trained at MGM Medical College in Mumbai and has been featured by the American Academy of Ophthalmology, has been working to counter common myths. Among the most harmful: the belief that laser treatment restores lost vision.

In reality, laser therapy for diabetic retinopathy is designed to prevent further vision loss by cauterizing abnormal blood vessels — not to reverse existing damage. Scatter laser therapy can preserve remaining sight, but side effects include permanent decreases in peripheral and color vision. Early intervention produces far better outcomes, which is precisely why screening before symptoms appear is critical.

Another persistent myth is that only severe cases require attention. In fact, even mild retinopathy demands monitoring, as it can progress rapidly and unpredictably. Anti-VEGF injections have emerged as a first-line therapy for moderate to severe diabetic macular edema, though milder forms may be managed with focal laser treatment and systemic glucose control.

What the Diaspora Should Know

South Asians develop Type 2 diabetes at younger ages and lower body weights compared to other populations, often before they would typically be screened. The American Diabetes Association recommends a comprehensive dilated eye exam at least annually for all diabetes patients, with more frequent monitoring for those showing early signs of retinopathy.

For NRIs managing diabetes, the message from specialists is clear: screening should begin at diagnosis, not when symptoms appear. With AI-powered tools now expanding access in India and established screening infrastructure in the US, UK, and Canada, the technology to prevent diabetic blindness exists. The challenge is getting patients through the door before it is too late.
